title: Education – And Its Limits (Gresham College, The Future of Work series)
author: Daniel Susskind

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts the need to reconstruct junior-lawyer development and materially extends the cluster’s proposed simulation response. It offers a concrete AI-enabled dispute simulation—complete with generated materials, clients, opponents and judges—and grounds the approach in established simulation practices from safety-critical engineering fields. It does not, however, address whether simulation must be combined with mentorship, independent practice or supervised live matters.
qs: They could now, you know, take the leading role in a simulation of a leading dispute, handling AI generated materials, interacting with AI generated clients, arguing their cases against AI generated opposition in front of an AI generated judge.
In so many areas of engineering, people master their roles in a simulated environment before moving on to do the tasks in the real world.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI capability is uneven and cannot be relied on without critical human judgment. It materially extends the cluster by proposing personalised and simulated learning—especially AI-generated legal simulations—as a concrete response to the risk that automation removes junior lawyers’ routine work and associated apprenticeship opportunities.
qs: And that's why in my view teaching people to make critical use of these technologies to not only understand how to use them but also how to understand their limitations their weaknesses uh their shortcomings is is incredibly important.

They could now, you know, take the leading role in a simulation of a leading dispute, handling AI generated materials, interacting with AI generated clients, arguing their cases against AI generated opposition in front of an AI generated judge.

st.t: Automation education: Adaptability helps but cannot suffice
st.an: Susskind directly supports the cluster’s proposition: education is the best near-term response to skills-related frictional unemployment, but it cannot address geographic or identity barriers, a future shortage of work, loss of purpose, or technology companies’ political power.
qs: The reason though this breakdown is important though is because if you think about it, education, more education is only really a response to the skills mismatch.

kp.k: Education addresses current frictional unemployment, not necessarily job scarcity
kp.d: Susskind distinguishes structural technological unemployment, where insufficient jobs exist, from frictional technological unemployment, where people cannot move into available work. He argues that frictional unemployment is the main current and medium-run challenge, making education the best available response, especially to skills mismatch. He situates generative AI within decades of technological encroachment on work and argues that the historical response of expanding educational participation and then advanced education now requires redesign.
qs: The first is what I've called structural technological unemployment. And here there just aren't enough jobs to be done full stop.

But there's also a second type of technological unemployment, a frictional one, where there are jobs, but for various important reasons, people are not able to move into those jobs to take up the work that is available.
But what I want to explain is why the meaning of more education has to change given the nature of the technological changes that are taking place.

kp.k: Coding illustrates the fragility of futureproofing strategies
kp.d: Susskind uses policies promoting coding as protection against automation to challenge the premise that durable, AI-resistant skills can be identified. He cites England's 2014 coding mandate, Finland's replacement of long division with coding in 2016, and Biden's 2019 recommendation that miners learn programming. Against these expectations, he reports an Anthropic founder's March 2025 prediction that AI would write 90% of code within 3 to 6 months and essentially all code within 12 months. Separately, he reports Anthropic's January claim that Claude Code wrote 90% of its own underlying code; this is a company-specific report, not evidence that the economy-wide prediction materialised.
qs: This year, England became the first country in the world to mandate teaching coding to children at primary and secondary schools.
We simply do not know enough about the relevant skills of the future to be telling young people that they ought to remake their entire career, their entire lives in pursuit of them.
Anthropic reported that 90% of the code behind Claude code which is their code uh AI powered coding assistant 90% of the code behind this system was itself written by Claude code.

kp.k: Prepare people for uncertainty rather than predicting protected skills
kp.d: Susskind rejects futureproofing as a pervasive but increasingly illusory strategy used by policymakers, employers, researchers, advisers and parents. He argues that the scale and unpredictability of technological change make confident identification of future valuable skills impossible. As another illustration, he contrasts a mathematician's April 2025 AI-related April Fool's joke with a subsequent OpenAI report of solving a prominent geometry problem, while acknowledging that the mathematician was already at the forefront of AI use. His recommendation is to treat uncertainty as a given and prepare people to navigate it.
qs: the fundamental problem that we face at the moment in the world of work is one of uncertainty.
I think we are spending far too much effort at the moment trying to resolve this uncertainty
to prepare them to navigate this extraordinary uncertainty that we currently face rather than attempting to resolve it.

kp.k: Foundational skills remain valuable despite uncertain future occupational demands
kp.d: Susskind recommends prioritising literacy, numeracy and critical thinking because they underpin the acquisition of other skills, rather than because they are immune to automation. He characterises mastery of these foundations as a no-regret strategy under uncertainty. His concern is that easy delegation to AI could cause people to stop practising and eventually forget these capabilities.
qs: My worry about AI um is that is it is going to lead us to just simply forget some of these basic skills altogether.
whatever they turn out to be they are going to rely in some way on those basic skills of literacy, numeracy and critical thinking.
It's a strategy that we aren't going to regret however the world turns out, however the uncertainty that we face um, resolves itself.

kp.k: Reported skills declines predate generative AI
kp.d: Susskind describes OECD PISA results as showing little change in basic skills between 2000 and 2009, followed by declines. He describes the latest round as published in 2022, covering 81 countries and 700,000 students aged 15, and reports a similar downward trend among adults in PIAAC. He attributes the proposed association with social media features introduced around 2009 to critics of social media; AI worsening these trends is his concern, not a finding established by those assessments.
qs: in the latest round published in in 2022 just to give you a flavor there were 81 countries involved 700,000 students took part
There are many people who point to that decline in basic skills among young people starting in 2009 as being um uh associated with the increasing use of of social media.
the OECD also do a very similar exercise, the PI AAC uh for adults, and you see a very similar downward trend in uh basic skills.

kp.k: Critical AI education must address fabricated legal authorities
kp.d: Susskind proposes devoting a third of educational time across primary, secondary, university and professional settings to effective AI use, paired with understanding its limitations. He reports a collection of almost one and a half thousand legal decisions involving generative-AI hallucinated content, describing lawyers relying on nonexistent cases. This is a reported collection of incidents, not a measured model error rate. He stresses that AI cannot be trusted like a calculator and identifies the unresolved educational challenge of teaching effective use without undermining foundational skills.
qs: I think we ought to be spending a third of our time in education whether it's primary, secondary, university, professional institutions teaching people in each of these different settings how to make effective use of these technologies.

he's found almost one and a half thousand cases where lawyers have used generative AI to inform their legal arguments only to have those only for it to turn out that some of the cases those arguments have relied upon have been hallucinated, have been entirely made up.
How do we teach people to use AI effectively without also undermining uh those basic skills that we think are really valuable and important?

kp.k: AI tutoring could expand access to personalised instruction
kp.d: Susskind invokes Benjamin Bloom's early-1980s two-sigma finding that an average individually tutored student tends to outperform 98% of students in traditional classrooms. He argues that AI could address the cost barrier to scaling such instruction, citing Khan Academy's partnership with OpenAI and its tutoring chatbot. His judgment that current systems explain and guide more effectively than many teachers, including himself, is presented as personal experience, not a comparative study establishing equivalent AI learning gains. Examples range from explaining human origins to a five-year-old to a colleague's account of solving and explaining the Ramsey growth model.
qs: an average student who receives onetoone tuition will tend to outperform almost everyone 98% of students in a traditional classroom setting.
providing everyone with a human tutor is extraordinarily expensive.
That is more effective in my view than many of the teachers I've watched in action over the years and I include myself in that.

kp.k: Simulated legal practice could accelerate junior lawyers' development
kp.d: Drawing an analogy with nuclear operations, astronaut training and engineering simulations, Susskind proposes AI-generated professional learning environments. He describes junior lawyers spending their first 5 to 10 years on routine document assembly, retrieval and review, and suggests that simulated disputes could instead give them early experience leading matters. AI-generated materials, clients, opponents and judges would expose trainees to work traditionally encountered much later, if at all. This is a proposed training model, not an evaluated implementation.
qs: Think of a junior lawyer for instance who spends the first 5 to 10 years of their career doing relatively routine work, document assembly, document retrieval, document uh review.

They could now, you know, take the leading role in a simulation of a leading dispute, handling AI generated materials, interacting with AI generated clients, arguing their cases against AI generated opposition in front of an AI generated judge.
they could engage in the sorts of opportunities to learn their trade that would traditionally come far later in their career, if at all.

kp.k: Lifelong retraining requires rebalancing heavily frontloaded educational investment
kp.d: Susskind argues that uncertainty requires serious opportunities to retrain throughout adulthood, rather than concentrating investment at life's beginning. He reports US annual public-school spending of about $18,000 per pupil from ages five to 18, potentially $32,000 in New York, followed by average annual support of $13,000 for undergraduates and 115,000 for graduates as transcribed, excluding subsidised state loans. He contrasts these figures with approximately $10 annually for adult state-funded programmes and describes Singapore's Skills Future as offering one-off credits worth about $3,000 after age 40. He also stresses that adult education's organisation, not only its funding, needs reform.
qs: As an adult, you might receive on average $10 a year through state funded programs if you're lucky to get anything at all.
Skills Future, it still only provides oneoff credits worth about $3,000 when you're over 40.
a willingness and a capacity to retrain and reskill later in life with the same intensity and seriousness with which we currently engage in education at the start of our lives.

kp.k: Education cannot resolve every barrier to available employment
kp.d: Susskind identifies three causes of frictional technological unemployment: inadequate skills, geographic separation from jobs, and identities that conflict with available work. He argues that education as currently understood principally addresses the first, not the latter two. He further argues that education alone cannot answer structural unemployment, which he treats as a scenario worth taking seriously further into the 21st century rather than the present main challenge.
qs: education, more education is only really a response to the skills mismatch.
the work that's available isn't the sort of work that they think people like them ought to be doing.
not simply is it a partial response to frictional technological unemployment but it's not a response at all to the structural technological unemployment.

kp.k: Potential work scarcity calls for greater state redistribution
kp.d: Conditional on a future with insufficient paid work, Susskind identifies inequality as a central economic problem: wages would become less effective at distributing society's income. He advocates a larger state role in sharing technological prosperity, explicitly distinguishing redistribution from centralised command of production. This is a proposed response to a future scenario, not a claim that education has already ceased to support employment.
qs: How do we share our income in society if our traditional way of doing so, paying people for the work that they do, is less effective than it has been in the past?
It's not a big state of production. It's a big state of distribution.

kp.k: Social contribution may need recognition beyond paid employment
kp.d: Susskind argues that social solidarity currently rests partly on people contributing through work and taxes, with job-search expectations attached to state support. If sufficient well-paid work disappears, he proposes opportunities for socially meaningful noneconomic contributions that others can recognise. He sees this contributive challenge as requiring measures beyond skills education.
qs: Today's social solidarity comes from a feeling that everybody is pulling their economic weight through the work that they do and the taxes that they pay.

providing people with the opportunity to make noneconomic contributions to society to do other types of work which we think is socially valuable, socially meaningful and important even if it's not paid work in the labor market.

kp.k: Technology companies' political power exceeds existing regulatory frameworks
kp.d: Susskind predicts that concern about major technology companies will increasingly centre on political power and its effects on liberty, justice and democracy, rather than economic power alone. He regards competition policy and antitrust law as useful for identifying and addressing economic concentration but argues that tools for identifying and intervening against political power abuses are largely missing. Education is not, in his account, an adequate response to this governance challenge.
qs: our main concern with large technology companies is going to be far more with their political power and the impact they have on things like liberty, justice, democracy, and whether those things are under threat.
we've got almost nothing available to us as a toolkit for helping us identify uses and abuses of political power

kp.k: Reduced employment raises questions of purpose and leisure policy
kp.d: Susskind argues that a future with less paid work could remove not only income but also direction, fulfilment and structure. He questions whether education oriented towards labour-market success addresses this loss and proposes considering leisure policies that shape nonworking lives. The argument remains conditional on paid work losing its central role.
qs: work, it's often said, is not simply a source of income, but it's also a source of direction and fulfillment.
Do we need to start thinking about leisure policies, how we intervene to shape people's non-working lives instead?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Susskind argues that AI makes future skill requirements uncertain, requiring redesigned education rather than promises of future-proof careers. He identifies opportunities for AI tutoring and simulated professional training, alongside risks of fabricated legal material and erosion of foundational skills.
pts.d: In this cross-domain lecture, Daniel Susskind argues that increasingly capable technologies are taking on tasks previously considered exclusively human. He treats reliably identifying future-proof skills as impossible, using coding and mathematics to illustrate uncertainty rather than establishing a forecast of particular occupational losses. His proposed educational response combines literacy, numeracy and critical thinking with effective but critical AI use; he proposes devoting a third of educational time to learning effective use across primary, secondary, university and professional settings. He worries that reliance on AI will lead people to forget foundational skills. He claims current AI can provide low-cost personalized instruction, in his experience more effectively than many teachers. For law specifically, he proposes simulations in which junior lawyers handle major disputes, AI-generated materials, clients, opponents and judges, gaining experiences normally available much later, if at all. He also warns that generative AI fabricates legal authorities and cannot be trusted like a calculator. More broadly, education addresses skills mismatch but not all geographical or identity-related barriers to employment, and cannot by itself solve a future shortage of work. Under that latter scenario, he calls for greater state redistribution, opportunities for noneconomic contribution, responses to technology companies' political power, and attention to meaning and nonworking lives.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The lecture draws on historical policy examples, reported AI achievements, educational research, international skills assessments, a legal hallucination case collection and personal experience; several proposals and predictions remain illustrative rather than empirically demonstrated.
pts.d: For uncertainty about future-proof skills, Susskind contrasts coding education policies with AI coding progress, including Anthropic's reported January figure that Claude Code wrote 90% of its own code. The March 2025 prediction about AI writing almost all code is a quoted company founder's forecast, not an independently established finding or Susskind's own quantified prediction. He also cites an OpenAI report of solving a combinatorial geometry problem and Timothy Gowers's reactions, while acknowledging that Gowers was already at the forefront of AI use in mathematics. For skill erosion, he cites OECD PISA and adult PIAAC declines that predate generative AI; these support a pre-existing trend, not a measured causal effect of AI. For legal reliability, he reports a collector's almost 1,500 legal decisions involving hallucinated AI content; this is a case collection, not a model error-rate benchmark. For tutoring, he cites Benjamin Bloom's two-sigma result concerning human one-to-one tuition, describes Khanmigo, and offers his own experience and an economist colleague's account of AI explaining the Ramsey growth model. The Bloom result is not presented as a measured result for AI tutors. His junior-lawyer simulation proposal relies on analogy with engineering training and his assessment of current technical feasibility, without reported legal-training outcome data. Spending comparisons and a referenced Harvard report support his argument that adult education is underfunded and poorly organized. The structural unemployment scenario and wider social responses are conceptual arguments, with references to previous lectures rather than new labour-market estimates.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Susskind distinguishes current and medium-run skills and mobility problems from a conditional longer-term shortage of work; he presents AI tutoring and professional simulation as current possibilities, not proven universal replacements.
pts.d: For now and the medium run, Susskind identifies frictional technological unemployment as the main challenge and more education as the best available response. He says the technology for broader simulated learning is now available and describes junior lawyers accessing experiences otherwise delayed through their first five to ten years of routine work. The coding example spans educational policy changes in the 2010s, a quoted March 2025 company forecast and a January report described as occurring 'this year' in the document labelled 2026. The mathematics example is framed relative to recent reports rather than a precise independently specified date. His concern about AI eroding skills is prospective; the educational declines he cites began earlier. Claims about effective AI use are qualified by serious flaws and the need to understand limitations while protecting basic skills. Structural technological unemployment is explicitly not his diagnosis of the present: he treats it as a scenario to take seriously further into the twenty-first century. Redistribution and other post-work responses are conditional on that scenario, not predictions that all paid work will disappear on a specified date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups include junior lawyers, lawyers relying on AI-generated authorities, learners and educators at all stages, workers needing retraining, and the wider public under possible longer-term labour-market disruption.
pts.d: Junior lawyers could gain earlier access to demanding dispute-handling practice through simulation rather than spending their early careers only on routine tasks. Lawyers using AI to formulate arguments face the risk of relying on nonexistent cases; the lecture does not quantify this risk by firm type or legal market segment. Children, students and adult learners could gain inexpensive personalized assistance but also risk losing literacy, numeracy and critical-thinking skills through overreliance. Teachers and professional institutions would need to change educational content and delivery; Susskind does not predict wholesale teacher replacement. Existing workers and people entering or moving through the labour market need flexibility and serious opportunities to retrain throughout life. Governments and employers are implicated in abandoning overly confident skill forecasts and expanding adult learning. In the longer-term shortage-of-work scenario, the public faces challenges concerning income distribution, contribution, solidarity, meaning and political power. These are society-wide claims, not specific predictions about law-firm staffing, pricing or legal-service market shares.
